content.title: Bloodhounds season 2: K-pop star Rain joins boxing drama as the menacing villain
content.text: Lead cast: Woo Do-hwan, Lee Sang-yi, RainWoo Do-hwan (Mr. Plankton) and Lee Sang-yi (Spice Up Our Love) return as happy-go-lucky bruisers Gun-woo and Woo-jin in season two of the acclaimed Netflix action-drama Bloodhounds, directed by Kim Joo-hwan (also known as Jason Kim).The young boxers have trimmed their locks and risen up in the world, but their good intentions are once again thwarted by the arrival of a money-hungry villain, this time played by K-pop icon Rain (Red Swan).Following their battle with a vicious loan shark and his goons in season one, Gun-woo has returned to the ring, with Woo-jin by his side as his coach and housemate.The friends live with Gun-woo’s mother, Yoon So-yeon (Yoon Yoo-sun), in a sleek new house and help out at her suburban cafe when not preparing for Gun-woo’s coming world title bout.Gun-woo’s efforts pay off when he prevails against the aggressive world champion in the ring, but unfortunately for him and his family, his victory puts him on the radar of Im Baek-jeong (Rain), a fearsome boxer who runs a brutal bare-knuckle fight club.This underground tournament generates enormous betting revenue from millions of anonymous online viewers and rarely ends well for whoever loses the fight.Still basking in victory, Gun-woo and Woo-jin receive an unpleasant visit from Baek-jeong, flanked by his shady cronies, who offers Gun-woo a big payout to come fight in his illegal tournament. Not appreciating the threatening house call, they turn Baek-jeong down, knowing full well that this will not be the last they see of him.Woo Do-hwan in a still from Bloodhounds season 2. Photo: Soyun Jeon, Seowoo Jung/NetflixOnce again, Gun-woo and Woo-jin have to raise their fists to protect Gun-woo’s mother – whose business was also under threat in season one – as well as police officer Kang Tae-young (Park Ye-ni), who was injured last season.They are joined in this fight by their friends, including corporate heir Hong Min-beom (Choi Si-won) and loan shark and former marine Moon Gwang-mu (Park Hoon).The winning camaraderie between Gun-woo and Woo-jin, built on sincerity, justice and friendship, has largely been preserved, but judging by its first two episodes, Bloodhounds’ second outing is comparatively lightweight at a narrative level.The chummy leads are the oil that keeps the engine running, but without moral grey areas, the black-and-white conflict, though slick and effective, lacks the same emotional wallop.Lee Sang-yi in a still from Bloodhounds season 2. Photo: Soyun Jeon, Seowoo Jung/NetflixLast season, Gun-woo and Woo-jin were boxing adversaries before they teamed up, following which they entered the murky world of illegal moneylending. They began working for a benevolent loan shark and had a complicated relationship with his right-hand woman, played by the late Kim Sae-ron.There was no real mystery as to who was good or bad, but part of the pleasure was seeing the characters learn for themselves what each other’s values were. This emotional engagement added a live edge to the show’s breathless pacing and gruelling choreography.With season two, the villain and conflict are set up straight away and there is no real middle ground for the characters to navigate their way through. They are either on the attack or on the defensive – good for chases and set pieces, not so much for the character drama that would ideally link and lift those sequences.Thankfully, this new season delivers a truly menacing new antagonist, with Rain proving to be the surprise stand-out so far. Eyes forever frozen in an icy glare, Baek-jeong oozes danger whenever he appears, and his fists, fuelled by bloodlust, land with punishing force.(From left) Rain, Woo Do-hwan and Lee Sang-yi in a still from Bloodhounds season 2. Photo: Soyun Jeon, Seowoo Jung/NetflixThe combination of Rain’s broad physique and the thunderous fight choreography makes the character an electric presence on screen. The show is building to Gun-woo and Baek-jeong facing off, and when that does happen, the sparks will be sure to fly.Dating back to charming indies like Koala – about friends struggling to run a small eatery – director Kim’s brand of on-screen male camaraderie has always been lifted by earnestness and a sense of pragmatism. His bigger works, starting with Midnight Runners, have leveraged that signature style into grander action spectacles.That culminates in Bloodhounds, and the new season once again seeks to capitalise on that mix of bonding and brawling. But the result feels a little more clinical this time, partly owing to its modern suburban setting and conspicuous lifestyle-product placement – including a trip to big-box store Traders.What that amounts to is a continuation that is still hugely impactful, even if it pulls its punches when it comes to the story.Bloodhounds season 2 is streaming on Netflix.
